newsitem.title: KENYA: Ethnic poison feeds crisis in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Ethnic poison feeds crisis in Zaire.

text.p: Ethnic poison between Hutus and Tutsis in Central Africa is feeding the multi-sided war and humanitarian crisis in eastern Zaire. Outlines of the main groups in the region follow.
BANYAMULENGE - An estimated 300,000 ethnic Tutsis who moved to what is now eastern Zaire from Rwanda as long as 200 years ago but were denied Zairean citizenship in 1981.

They say Zairean authorities started persecuting them as ethnic Tutsis in 1994 when Rwandan Hutu refugees arrived, fleeing after the genocide in Rwanda. But they have long been mistrusted by local Zaireans.
Thousands of Banyamulenge crossed back into Rwanda during the genocide in 1994 and joined Tutsi-led Rwandan rebels who seized power and now dominate the Rwandan government army.

In the last few weeks they have launched a large-scale offensive against the Zaire army, scoring unexpected successes in cooperation with a range of rebel Zairean groups. The rebel forces now control Goma, Bukavu, Uvira and other areas.
Banyamulenge say their fighters are protecting their people from genocide planned by Zairean politicians and the army.
BANYARWANDA - Literally, "people of Rwanda". They include the Banyamulenge and anyone else in eastern Zaire whose origins were in Rwanda, whether Hutus, Tutsis or the tiny Twa minority.

When colonial powers drew borders in the Great Lakes region in the late 19th and early 20th century some Banyarwanda found themselves within the borders of the Belgian Congo (now Zaire), others in Uganda. In the 1920s and 1930s many Rwandans were taken to work on plantations in Belgian Congo, and many Rwandans crossed to Masisi, Zaire, as economic migrants.
Fighting between the local Banyarwanda, fleeing Rwandan Bahutu and local Zaireans was concentrated in the Masisi region of eastern Zaire earlier this year -- before the Banyamulenge revolt.
ZAIREAN ARMY - A notoriously ill-disciplined force, the Zairean army beefed up its presence in eastern Zaire in September following confrontation with the Banyamulenge.

When they suffer a military defeat or lose comrades, the troops frequently rampage through civilian centres, shooting in the air, looting vehicles and stealing to augment their small and rarely paid salaries.

ZAIREAN MILITIAS - The Bangilima and the Mai-Mai are Zairean militias with a strong background of witchcraft. A mix of local Zairean tribes including the Hunde, they oppose the Banyarwanda and have fought both Tutsis and Hutus.

They have fought Hutus because they fear the creation of a "Hutu land" in North Kivu, comprising property grabbed there by ethnic Zairean Hutus and Rwandan Hutu refugees with the collusion of the Zairean government and army.

The Bangilima and Mai-Mai have a tactical alliance with the Tutsis but could turn against them. The Bangilima are mainly from Lubero area. The Mai-Mai are so called because they say bullets fired at them will magically turn into water (mai).

RWANDAN REFUGEES - An estimated 1.1 million Rwandan Hutus fled their homeland in 1994 during the genocide of up to one million Tutsis and Hutu moderates by Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs. Most were housed in crowded camps around Goma, Bukavu and Uvira in eastern Zaire, with others in equally crowded camps in western Tanzania.

The Zairean government wants those on its territory to return home and has repeatedly threatened to expel them all. Tanzania has also called for their return. Most refugees have refused, saying they fear reprisals for the 1994 slaughter in Rwanda.

Hundreds of thousands of Rwandans have fled from the camps near Goma in the last few days, but the whereabouts of large numbers formerly in camps around Bukavu and Uvira are now unknown. The 600,000 in Tanzania are still in camps there.

Refugee camps in eastern Zaire near the border with Rwanda were also used as bases by former Rwandan Hutu militiamen, the Interahamwe, who played a leading role in the 1994 genocide and have threatened refugees against returning.
Eastern Zaire also has camps for the estimated 40,000 former Rwandan Hutu government troops who fled to Zaire. Rwanda accuses the Zairean government of backing exiled Hutu forces.
The former Rwandan Hutu soldiers recently fought alongside Zairean troops against Tutsi rebels attacking Goma and refugee camps in the Goma and Bukavu regions but had little success.

BURUNDIAN REFUGEES - An estimated 140,000 Burundian Hutus, most of whom lived in camps north of Uvira, in eastern Zaire on Burundi's western border, were scattered when Banyamulenge rebels took control of Uvira in October.
About 30,000 returned to Burundi, others fled across Lake Tanganyika in boats to Tanzania but 100,000 are missing.
The Zaire army has gained the upper hand in its war against Hutu rebels since the fall of Uvira, because rebels have lost control of their bases in the Uvira refugee camps.

RWANDAN ARMY - The 54,000-strong Rwanda Patriotic Army is dominated by the country's Tutsi minority, which seized power in July 1994 and ended the genocide launched by the Hutu majority three months earlier.
Its soldiers intervened in eastern Zaire earlier this month, crossing the border from the Rwandan town of Cyangugu into Bukavu at night to stop Zairean firing across the frontier.
Zaire accuses the armies of Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda of invading eastern Zaire to fight alongside Tutsi rebels to carve out a Tutsi homeland in its territory.
